message.content:
**The most iconic 19th‑century sculpture is generally considered to be *The Kiss* by Auguste Rodin (1889).** ### Why *The Kiss* stands out | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Date** | 1889 (late 19th century) | | **Artist** | Auguste Rodin, a leading figure of modern sculpture | | **Style** | Realist/Impressionist blend; dynamic, sensual, and emotionally charged | | **Impact** | • Became an instant visual icon, reproduced in countless editions and media.
• Influenced the transition from classical to modern sculpture.
• Continues to be one of the most recognized and reproduced works worldwide. | | **Legacy** | • Frequently cited in discussions of 19th‑century art history.
• Its themes of love and intimacy resonated with contemporary audiences and remain relevant today. | ### Other notable 19th‑century sculptures | Sculpture | Artist | Year | Significance | |-----------|--------|------|--------------| | *The Gates of Hell* | Rodin | 1880–1917 (unfinished) | Monumental, complex narrative; a landmark in sculptural storytelling. | | *The Thinker* | Rodin | 1902–1904 (early 20th century) | Iconic, but technically belongs to the 20th century. | | *The Birth of Venus* (re‑interpretations) | Various | 19th century revivals | Revived interest in Renaissance themes. | | *The Rape of the Sabine Women* | Antonio Canova | 1797–1807 (late 18th century) | Influential, but predates the 19th century. | ### Bottom line While many masterpieces were created during the 19th century, *The Kiss* by Rodin is the sculpture most frequently cited as the era’s defining work—its combination of technical mastery, emotional immediacy, and enduring popularity make it the quintessential 19th‑century sculpture.
